mcqs.question: A team asks "should we use a gateway or a mesh to handle traffic between our own internal services?" What's the issue with how the question is framed?
options: There's no issue — gateway and mesh are interchangeable for this use case
A gateway is built for north-south (edge) traffic, not internal east-west traffic — so for purely internal service-to-service traffic, a mesh is the relevant tool, not a choice between the two
Neither tool can handle internal traffic; a load balancer is required instead
The mesh is only for external traffic, so the gateway is actually the right answer
mcqs.explanation: The framing conflates two tools built for opposite traffic directions — a gateway simply isn't positioned to see or manage internal service-to-service calls, which is squarely the mesh's job. They aren't interchangeable, and a load balancer alone doesn't provide the mTLS/retry/observability concerns a mesh addresses.

mcqs.question: Why might a 5-service startup reasonably decide NOT to adopt a service mesh yet, even though a mesh has real benefits?
options: Because meshes only work with more than 100 services
Because at low service count, the mesh's added operational complexity (control plane, proxy hop per call) may outweigh benefits a simple shared library could deliver more cheaply
Because meshes are incompatible with startups' cloud providers
Because a gateway makes a mesh technically impossible to run
mcqs.explanation: The mesh decision is a cost-benefit call tied to scale: at low service count, a shared library or simple retry logic can deliver similar value without the operational overhead of running a mesh control plane and adding a proxy hop to every call. There's no hard service-count floor required by mesh software itself, no cloud-provider incompatibility, and a gateway doesn't block mesh adoption.

mcqs.question: In a system running both a gateway and a mesh, what happens to a client request after it's authenticated at the gateway?
options: It bypasses the mesh entirely and goes directly to a single backend service
It may fan out across multiple internal service-to-service calls, which the mesh secures (mTLS) and observes, separate from the gateway's edge-level work
The gateway re-authenticates the request again at every internal hop
The mesh re-authenticates the original external client at each internal service
mcqs.explanation: Once past the gateway, a request commonly triggers several internal calls between services — that's exactly the east-west traffic the mesh secures and observes, distinct from the gateway's one-time edge-level authentication. The gateway doesn't re-run per internal hop, and the mesh doesn't re-verify the original external client identity, since that's outside its scope.

mcqs.question: What is the mesh's structural blind spot that the gateway covers, and vice versa?
options: The mesh has no concept of the original external client once a request is inside; the gateway has zero visibility into internal service-to-service calls
Both layers see and secure exactly the same traffic, with no blind spots on either side
The gateway can't handle HTTPS; the mesh can't handle HTTP
The mesh only works for databases; the gateway only works for APIs
mcqs.explanation: Each layer's blind spot is the other's core job: the gateway has no insight into what happens after a request enters the system, and the mesh has no awareness of the original external caller — that's exactly why systems at scale run both rather than picking one. Neither tool has the protocol or workload-type limitations described in the other options.

mcqs.question: What's the main risk for a 200-service organization that decides to skip adopting a service mesh?
options: No risk — a gateway alone is always sufficient regardless of internal service count
Cross-cutting concerns like mTLS, retries, and observability end up implemented inconsistently and duplicated across many teams and languages instead of centralized
The organization would be unable to use an API gateway at all
All internal traffic would become publicly accessible from the internet
mcqs.explanation: At large scale, skipping a mesh means each team re-solves mTLS, retries, and observability independently, in whatever language and however consistently they choose — a maintenance and consistency risk that grows with service and team count. A gateway remains usable regardless, and skipping a mesh doesn't expose internal traffic to the public internet by itself.
